title: Scalar Subquery
description: Understand one-value subquery shape, zero-row NULL and multirow errors, and preserve lookup, aggregate and correlation contracts when rewriting queries.

questions.question_text: What must a scalar subquery return?
options: One selected column and at most one result row; zero rows yield NULL in MySQL
questions.explanation: Exactly one row is not required: zero rows become NULL, while more than one row causes a MySQL cardinality error.

questions.question_text: Where can a scalar subquery legally be used?
options: Supported scalar-expression contexts such as a SELECT-list value or a suitable WHERE comparison
questions.explanation: Supported expression contexts depend on the engine and clause; avoid an unrestricted anywhere claim.

questions.question_text: What does `(SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE name='Zack')` evaluate to if no employee named Zack exists?
questions.explanation: Zero rows returned by a scalar subquery yields NULL, not an error.

questions.question_text: If known salaries average 71250.00, what does an uncorrelated AVG subquery logically display beside each outer employee row?
options: A different value per row, matching that employee's department
The same value, 71250.00, repeated in every row
It errors because a subquery cannot appear in SELECT
questions.explanation: The same global benchmark appears beside every outer row; this does not guarantee a particular physical execution count.

questions.question_text: Which of these would be safely usable as a scalar subquery expression?
options: (SELECT department FROM employees) which can return 8 rows
questions.explanation: MAX with no GROUP BY always collapses to one row, one column — a safe scalar shape. The others have multiple columns or an unbounded row count.

questions.question_text: Which SQL clause is a scalar subquery for a company-wide average salary most naturally used in?
options: The SELECT list, as a computed column
The FROM clause as a table
questions.explanation: A common use of scalar subqueries is as a computed column alongside real columns.

questions.question_text: A scalar subquery must return at most:
questions.explanation: Both the row count and column count must be exactly one (or zero rows, which yields NULL).

questions.question_text: Why do aggregate functions like AVG/COUNT/SUM make excellent scalar subqueries?
options: They are always faster than joins
They collapse to a single row automatically when there is no GROUP BY, guaranteeing the scalar shape
They can only be used inside subqueries
They automatically ignore rows with NULL department
questions.explanation: An ordinary ungrouped aggregate SELECT supplies one aggregate row. GROUP BY or other shape-changing clauses require a separate cardinality check.

questions.question_text: What does a zero-row scalar subquery yield in MySQL?
questions.explanation: No scalar value row becomes a NULL expression.

questions.question_text: What happens when a scalar subquery returns two rows in MySQL?
questions.explanation: The scalar position requires at most one result row.

questions.question_text: Does a current unique display name prove future scalar lookup uniqueness?
options: Yes, one sample is a constraint
questions.explanation: A declared key or valid domain guarantee must establish cardinality.

questions.question_text: Why can LIMIT 1 conceal a data-contract problem?
options: It proves the table is normalized
It changes a uniqueness requirement into a selection rule
It removes every duplicate from storage
questions.explanation: Choosing one candidate is not the same as proving at most one exists.

questions.question_text: What does ungrouped COUNT return for no qualifying rows?
questions.explanation: COUNT produces its single aggregate row with zero.

questions.question_text: What does ungrouped AVG normally return for no known values?
questions.explanation: No known values leave the average undefined under ordinary aggregate behavior.

questions.question_text: Can a grouped aggregate return several rows?
options: No, all aggregate functions are scalar-shaped
questions.explanation: Each represented group contributes a row.

questions.question_text: What can an omitted correlation accidentally produce?
options: A correct per-parent value by default
The same global value for every outer row
questions.explanation: The subquery must tie its population to the intended outer identity.

questions.question_text: What can a join rewrite change if multiple children exist?
options: The number of letters in a table name
questions.explanation: A join emits matching pairs rather than preserving a scalar cardinality error.

questions.question_text: Does NULL rate alone identify a missing instructor?
options: No, a real instructor’s rate may also be NULL
Only when an alias is short
questions.explanation: Match absence and unknown matched value can share the same displayed NULL.

questions.question_text: Does an uncorrelated expression guarantee one physical execution?
options: No, inspect actual plan and engine behavior
questions.explanation: Logical semantics do not fix every physical execution choice.

questions.question_text: What must a rewrite preserve before performance comparison?
options: Identity, multiplicity, NULL and cardinality behavior
Only the order of table definitions
questions.explanation: Equivalent-looking syntax can answer a different question.

coding_problems.title: Display the global known salary average
coding_problems.task: Return instructor_id, salary, overall_average for every pay row. The average uses all known salaries and is cast to DECIMAL(10, 2). Order by instructor_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE instructor_pay(instructor_id INT PRIMARY KEY,salary INT NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT i.instructor_id,i.salary,(SELECT CAST(AVG(a.salary) AS DECIMAL(10,2)) FROM instructor_pay a) AS overall_average FROM instructor_pay i ORDER BY i.instructor_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The global aggregate uses known salaries while the outer projection retains all pay rows.

validation_cases.expected:
instructor_id	salary	overall_average
1	NULL	NULL
2	NULL	NULL

coding_problems.title: Count each instructor’s confirmed sessions
coding_problems.task: Return instructor_id, confirmed_count for every instructor using a scalar correlated aggregate. Only status confirmed counts. Order by instructor_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE instructors(instructor_id INT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE sessions(session_id INT PRIMARY KEY,instructor_id INT NULL,status VARCHAR(12));
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO instructors VALUES(1),(2),(3); INSERT INTO sessions VALUES(1,1,'confirmed'),(2,1,'confirmed'),(3,2,'cancelled'),(4,NULL,'confirmed');
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT i.instructor_id,(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sessions s WHERE s.instructor_id=i.instructor_id AND s.status='confirmed') AS confirmed_count FROM instructors i ORDER BY i.instructor_id;
hints: COUNT without GROUP BY returns zero for no matches.
coding_problems.explanation: Each outer instructor retains one row and gets a count from only their qualifying sessions.

notes:
## Supply one value rather than another row set

A scalar subquery is a parenthesized query used where the surrounding SQL context permits one value. It selects one column and must produce at most one row. In MySQL, a zero-row scalar subquery yields NULL, and a multirow result raises an error. This cardinality contract distinguishes it from a derived table in FROM and from predicates such as EXISTS that ask whether any qualifying row exists.

The word scalar does not mean the underlying query can examine only one source row. An ungrouped SUM can inspect many rows and return one total. A unique-key lookup can inspect an access path and return one value. A grouped query can return several rows even if it contains an aggregate. Determine the output shape from the query and constraints rather than assuming that parentheses or a familiar function name guarantee scalar behavior.

## Put a shared aggregate beside detail rows

Suppose a training center stores salary values for instructors. A report can display each instructor's own salary alongside the average of all known salaries in the same table. An uncorrelated aggregate subquery states that comparison population separately from the outer detail rows. The shared average is a logical value in every outer row, not a different departmental calculation unless the subquery is explicitly correlated to that department.

```sql
SELECT i.instructor_id,i.salary,
       (SELECT AVG(a.salary) FROM instructor_pay a) AS overall_average
FROM instructor_pay i
ORDER BY i.instructor_id;
```

For salaries sixty, eighty and NULL, the average of known values is seventy. Each of the three outer instructor rows displays that same average, including the instructor whose own salary is NULL. The aggregate ignores the missing salary in its denominator, but the outer projection does not remove that instructor. If the outer table is empty, there are no detail rows on which to display the aggregate.

The logical repetition of the value is not a guarantee about a fixed number of physical executions. An optimizer can transform or cache eligible expressions according to its plan. Explain the result semantics first, and inspect a representative execution plan before claiming the query computes the average once physically or reruns it for every output row.

## Use uniqueness to prove a lookup's shape

A scalar lookup on an enforced unique identifier returns at most one row. A lookup by a nonunique display name has no such guarantee. Two instructors named Mira can make a salary-by-name scalar expression fail even if the original sample contained only one Mira. Current sample uniqueness is weaker than a declared domain key.

```sql
SELECT r.request_id,
       (SELECT i.hourly_rate
        FROM instructors i
        WHERE i.instructor_id=r.instructor_id) AS rate
FROM requests r
ORDER BY r.request_id;
```

This example assumes instructor_id is a key of instructors. A missing referenced instructor yields NULL for rate in the scalar expression. A real matched instructor can also have a nullable hourly_rate, so NULL alone does not distinguish absence from a known row with an unknown rate. If the workflow needs that distinction, return suitable match information through an appropriate join or another explicitly designed result contract.

## Predict zero rows and multirow failures

A query selecting one value for a nonexistent identity returns no rows, which becomes NULL in a scalar position. It does not become zero or an empty string. Comparing an outer amount with that NULL produces UNKNOWN under ordinary comparison semantics, and WHERE does not retain UNKNOWN. A missing benchmark can therefore remove every candidate unless the query defines a different policy deliberately.

A multirow scalar result is an error in MySQL. Do not conceal it by adding LIMIT 1 without a defined business selection rule. Without an appropriate ORDER BY, the selected row can be arbitrary. Even an ordered first row changes the contract from there must be at most one relevant row to choose this particular candidate among several. That change needs a requirement, not merely a desire to suppress an exception.

## Distinguish an aggregate row from no aggregate group

An aggregate query without GROUP BY ordinarily returns one aggregate row even when its input has no qualifying rows. COUNT returns zero for that input, while SUM and AVG normally return NULL. A grouped query returns one row per represented group and can therefore yield zero rows or several rows. Both the number of groups and the number of selected columns matter when embedding it as a scalar expression.

```sql
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM requests WHERE status='confirmed')
         AS confirmed_requests;
```

With no confirmed requests, the outer one-row query returns zero. By contrast, a scalar SELECT amount from a missing request returns NULL. A grouped count by instructor can produce several counts and fail in a scalar context. The presence of COUNT is not enough to establish scalar shape if GROUP BY or another row-producing construction remains.

## Correlate at the intended outer grain

A correlated scalar subquery refers to an outer row. For each instructor, a count of that instructor's confirmed sessions can be expressed with a correlation on the instructor key. The result is zero for an instructor with no qualifying sessions because the ungrouped count still returns its aggregate row. Omitting the correlation instead repeats the global count and answers a different question.

Use aliases that make each reference's owner visible. A mistaken unqualified identifier can bind to a local column when the author intended an outer one. Test at least two instructors with different child populations, a parent with no children, and a child with a missing or unrelated key where the schema permits it. A single parent fixture can fail to expose an omitted correlation.

## Rewrite with joins only after preserving the contract

A join can expose several related columns and may be clearer for that result. However, an unrestricted join can multiply outer rows where a scalar lookup would have raised a multirow error. A left join to a grouped count can yield NULL for a missing group where an ungrouped correlated count yielded zero. COALESCE may preserve the intended zero, but only after the desired missing-value policy is established.

A rewrite must preserve selected identities, duplicates, NULL behavior and cardinality constraints before it is compared for speed. An outer row repeated because of multiple children is not the same result as one scalar value per parent. DISTINCT may hide some repeated projections while still masking an incorrect intermediate grain or collapsing different people with identical display values.

## Keep type and syntax context explicit

The scalar expression has a result type derived from its selected value. Comparing text with numbers can invoke engine-specific conversion and produce surprising matches. Make units and types compatible rather than relying on incidental fixture values. A nullable lookup also needs a deliberate presentation policy; labeling a missing rate as free by replacing NULL with zero changes the business meaning.

Not every syntactic position that displays a number accepts an arbitrary scalar subquery. Engine-specific restrictions apply to clauses and statement forms. Use documented supported expression contexts such as the SELECT list and suitable WHERE comparisons rather than claiming that subqueries work in every conceivable value slot. Label MySQL-specific behavior and verify the target version when moving the expression into administrative or specialized syntax.

Test absence, multiple matches and all-NULL measures independently. These cases challenge different parts of the scalar contract and should not be collapsed into one generic empty-data example.

## Solve two scalar-value exercises

First exercise: return each pay row with the global average of known salaries. On sixty, eighty and NULL, the benchmark is seventy beside every retained outer row. Then make the input empty and explain why there are no outer detail rows, despite the aggregate query itself having a one-row shape. Retain identifiers so repeated salaries do not collapse separate instructors.

Second exercise: return every instructor and their confirmed-session count through a correlated ungrouped COUNT. An instructor with only cancelled sessions and one with no sessions both receive zero. Add duplicate qualifying child evidence with distinct session identifiers and verify that the count grows. Continue with [single-row subqueries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/single-row-subquery), [subqueries versus joins](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/subquery-vs-join) and [correlated subqueries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/correlated-subquery) to check shape, meaning and execution evidence separately.
